Female red king crabs (Paralithodes camtschaticus) produce a single large brood of eggs annually, with clutch sizes that can reach several thousand eggs. This species demonstrates a distinct thermal dependence in its early life history, with eggs incubated at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] requiring approximately 360 days [ab = approximately 360 days] to hatch. The newly emerged larvae possess a wet birth mass of 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], reflecting their diminutive size during the initial free-swimming stage. After hatching, these zoea larvae begin a pelagic phase that continues until the time from birth to metamorphosis reaches roughly 62 days  when reared at 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C], at which point they undergo the dramatic morphological transformation into glaucothoe and subsequently into benthic juveniles. The dry mass of individuals measured immediately after settlement and metamorphosis is approximately 0.001 grams , representing a significant accumulation of tissue during the planktonic feeding period. These early life stages are characterized by extremely high mortality rates in the wild, and only a tiny fraction of the thousands of larvae released per brood survive to recruit into the adult benthic population.

The onset of reproductive capability in this lithodid crab is tightly linked to carapace size rather than chronological age alone, a pattern observed across many decapod crustaceans. Females reach puberty at a carapace length of 9.7 centimeters [Lp = 9.7 centimeters], while males typically undergo sexual maturation at a somewhat larger carapace size, with puberty occurring at a carapace length of 10.5 centimeters [Lp = 10.5 centimeters]. This size dimorphism at maturity reflects divergent selective pressures on the sexes, with males often competing for access to receptive females. The body mass at which individuals typically reach reproductive maturity is substantial, with the wet weight at puberty calculated to be 840 grams [Wwp = 840 grams], a threshold derived from the scaling relationship between carapace length and body mass in this species. Comparative studies of congeneric species such as Paralithodes platypus suggest that this size threshold may vary with local environmental conditions and population density. The timing of this transition from juvenile to adult is delayed in colder waters, and under the thermal conditions of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] commonly observed in their Bering Sea habitat, the time from metamorphosis to puberty extends to approximately 6 years [tp = approximately 6 years].

Adult red king crabs exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size. Females grow to a maximum recorded wet weight of 8,000 grams [Wwi = 8,000 grams], whereas males can attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 10,000 grams [Wwi = 10,000 grams]. This difference is accompanied by a remarkable leg span, which in the largest males can reach 1.8 meters, a dimension that facilitates their movements across the soft-bottom substrates of the continental shelf. The ultimate carapace length of the largest documented individuals approaches 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters], placing this species among the largest of the king crabs. These maximum sizes, however, are rarely achieved in heavily exploited populations, where size-selective fishing removes the oldest and largest individuals. The growth pattern follows a decelerating trajectory, with young juveniles molting several times annually and adults molting only once per year or even less frequently as they approach their asymptotic dimensions.

The maximum reproductive output of this species is considerable and occurs under favorable conditions. At a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the highest recorded spawning frequency approaches roughly 11,000 eggs per day, a metric that reflects both the production of an enormous single clutch of approximately 150,000 to 400,000 eggs per reproductive event, combined with the potential for a female to produce one clutch annually. This peak fecundity is attained only by the largest, most fecund females and is contingent upon adequate food resources during the critical months preceding egg extrusion. The eggs are brooded externally, attached to the pleopods of the female for the duration of the roughly 12-month incubation period before hatching. Field surveys from the eastern Bering Sea indicate that reproductive success is highly variable among years, correlating closely with the abundance of calcareous shell-building organisms that serve as both prey and settlement habitat for juveniles.

Longevity in this commercially valuable species is considerable, with the maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions being approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when maintained at 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of slow-growing, late-maturing decapods that inhabit high-latitude environments with pronounced seasonal productivity pulses. The protracted developmental schedule, from the larval stage through the attainment of sexual maturity and into senescence, reflects the energetic challenges of life in cold, seasonally food-limited waters. Data from tag-recapture studies and analysis of gastric mill band counts have confirmed ages exceeding two decades for the largest males, though females tend to have somewhat shorter maximum lifespans due to the energetic demands of repeated reproductive cycles. The combination of late maturity, low natural mortality after recruitment, and high fecundity aligns with a life-history strategy typical of a K-selected benthic predator, one that is particularly vulnerable to overexploitation.
